papers.title: Acoustic Priors from the Latest Cosmic Microwave Background Data
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33334v1

summary.one_liner: Using a separation of early-Universe acoustic-peak information from late-time lensing and ISW effects, the paper updates model-independent CMB constraints on the acoustic scale and physical densities with Planck PR4, ACT DR6 and SPT-3G D1 data, and tests how marginalizing over lensing-induced peak smoothing affects the evidence for evolving dark energy from CMB plus DESI DR2 BAO.
summary.plain: The paper looks at the faint pattern of hot and cold spots in the leftover glow from the early Universe, the cosmic microwave background. It separates the part of that pattern that records conditions just after the Big Bang from distortions added on the way to us by gravity from large-scale structure. Using newer telescope data combined, the authors report updated measurements of the pattern's characteristic size and of the amounts of baryons and dark matter, and they study how these choices change the statistical case for dark energy changing over time.
summary.why: The claimed shift in dark-energy evidence, from 3.0 to 1.9 sigma (and 3.2 to 2.4 sigma with supernovae added), depends on modelling choices, so it matters for how strongly current data favour non-constant dark energy. The paper's own statements are limited to these analysis results; their wider significance is for specialists to judge.
summary.background:
- Cosmic microwave background (CMB): light from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, mapped as temperature and polarization patterns.
- Acoustic peaks: regularly spaced features in the CMB power spectrum, produced by sound waves in the early plasma; their spacing sets the angular acoustic scale.
- Gravitational lensing of the CMB: nearby matter bends the light, smoothing the peaks; the lensing signal can be reconstructed from the data.
- Integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect: a late-time shift in CMB photon energies caused by changing gravitational potentials, e.g. from dark energy.
- Physical densities (omega_b, omega_bc): baryon density and baryon-plus-dark-matter density, scaled by the Hubble constant squared.
- Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO): a preferred separation between galaxies left by early sound waves, used as a cosmic ruler; DESI DR2 is a recent survey.
- LCDM vs w0waCDM: the standard model with a constant dark energy versus a model where dark energy evolves over time; sigma values measure how strongly data prefer one over the other.
- Planck PR4, ACT DR6, SPT-3G D1, WMAP: CMB experiments and their data releases.

papers.abstract: We revisit the physics of the acoustic peaks and illustrate how early-Universe information in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be disentangled from late-time signatures imprinted by gravitational lensing and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. Applying this separation to Planck PR4, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 temperature and polarization data combined with the joint lensing reconstruction, we update the model-independent constraints on the angular acoustic scale and the physical densities, $100\theta_*=1.04100\pm0.00021$, $\omega_{\rm b}=(2.2440\pm0.0099)\times10^{-2}$, and $\omega_{\rm bc}=0.1410\pm0.0011$. These constraints are consistent with the previous Planck PR4-only analysis and remain stable for extended late-time cosmologies beyond $\Lambda$CDM. Adding ACT DR6 to the combination favors a higher $\omega_{\rm b}$ and, through their correlation, a higher primordial tilt $n_{\rm s}$ than PR4 alone. The reconstructed lensing spectrum exceeds that of $\Lambda$CDM, with two features near $L\simeq50$ and $L\sim10^3$, and the excess is reduced when WMAP replaces the Planck primary spectra. Marginalizing over the lensing-induced peak smoothing, rather than tying it to the late-time model, lowers the preference of the CMB and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) for $w_0w_a$CDM over $\Lambda$CDM from $3.0\sigma$ to $1.9\sigma$, or from $3.2\sigma$ to $2.4\sigma$ when Union3.1 supernovae are added. We further use the acoustic prior to predict BAO distances from CMB data alone under several late-time expansion histories, testing their consistency with DESI measurements assuming standard pre-recombination physics.

papers.title: No Cluster Left Behind I: Joint Mass Calibration for Dark Energy Survey and South Pole Telescope Clusters
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33522v1

summary.one_liner: A joint statistical model that combines Dark Energy Survey optical richness and weak-lensing data with South Pole Telescope Sunyaev-Zel'dovich signals to calibrate cluster masses, including clusters seen by only one survey, and to constrain optical selection biases.
summary.plain: Galaxy clusters are the largest gravitationally bound objects in the universe, and knowing their masses is key to measuring dark energy. This paper proposes a flexible way to combine cluster catalogs from different telescopes, so that clusters seen by only one survey can still be used. As a test, the authors combine optical galaxy counts and lensing measurements from the Dark Energy Survey with microwave signals from the South Pole Telescope.
summary.why: Mass calibration is a major source of uncertainty in cluster-based dark energy measurements, so a method that uses far more clusters could tighten those results. The text reports a roughly 20% bias in the large-scale lensing signal for richness-selected clusters, but the wider impact for next-generation surveys is the authors' claim and has not been tested here.
summary.background:
- Galaxy clusters: huge collections of galaxies and hot gas; their abundance depends on dark energy and matter.
- Mass calibration: working out how massive a cluster is, which is hard to measure directly.
- Richness: a count of member galaxies seen in optical images; cheap to measure but can be fooled by chance alignments along the line of sight.
- Weak lensing: faint distortion of background galaxy images by a cluster's gravity, used to estimate mass.
- Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect: a distortion of the cosmic microwave background caused by hot gas in clusters, detected by the South Pole Telescope.
- Selection bias: systematic errors from how a sample of objects was chosen.
- Halo mass function: how many clusters of each mass exist, a key cosmological test.

papers.abstract: Multiwavelength observations of galaxy clusters are among the most promising probes of the growth of structure and dark energy. Optically identified clusters have a high number density and can thus probe the halo mass function well into the group regime, but their weak-lensing mass calibration suffers from a selection bias induced by line-of-sight projection effects. Clusters detected via their intracluster medium (ICM) -- through X-ray emission or the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZe) -- are less affected by such selection biases, but current survey sensitivity restricts ICM-selected samples to high-mass systems. Previous multiwavelength analyses tend to limit to clusters with millimeter detections and thus to the high-mass population. In this paper, we propose a flexible modeling framework in which all clusters from multiwavelength surveys can be combined and modeled, even if they are detected in only one survey. As a pilot study, we jointly model richness and lensing of clusters from the Dark Energy Survey and the SZe signal from the South Pole Telescope. This approach yields precise cluster mass calibration while self-consistently constraining optical selection biases. We have found a $\sim$20% bias in the large-scale lensing signal of clusters selected by richness, and a bias ranging from $\sim-20$% at low richness to zero at high richness for clusters selected by both richness and SZe. Compared to current approaches, this framework is highly scalable and readily extensible, paving the way for the full utilization of multiwavelength cluster data in next-generation surveys.

papers.title: Black hole accretion flows as dark matter bolometers
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34172v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies; its particle nature is unknown.
- Direct-detection experiments: lab detectors that wait for dark matter particles to bump into atoms.
- Bolometer: a device that measures energy by sensing a temperature rise; here the dark matter acts as a heat sink for electrons.
- Accretion flow: hot gas spiralling inward toward a black hole, emitting light as it heats up.
- Advection-dominated accretion flow (ADAF): a thin, very hot, low-density model of such gas in which the electrons and ions are at different temperatures.
- M87*: the supermassive black hole at the centre of galaxy M87, first imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope.
- Sub-MeV / keV-to-MeV: particle masses of thousandths to millions of electron-volts, far lighter than a proton.
- Mediator: the hypothetical particle that carries the force between dark matter and ordinary matter; "heavy" and "light" mediators give different interaction strengths.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes using the hot accretion flow around the supermassive black hole M87* as a calorimeter for light dark matter, integrating dark-matter cooling of electrons into the flow's thermodynamics and fitting the predicted radio-to-millimeter spectrum to Event Horizon Telescope-era observations to constrain dark matter-electron scattering for keV-to-MeV masses and both heavy and light mediators.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether gas falling onto the giant black hole at the center of galaxy M87 can reveal dark matter. The idea is that very light dark matter particles can carry heat away from the hot electrons in that gas, cooling them and slightly changing the radio and millimeter light the gas gives off. The authors model this cooling, compare the predicted light with observations made alongside the Event Horizon Telescope campaign, and use the mismatch limits to rule out some dark matter interaction strengths.

papers.abstract: Astrophysical systems provide powerful probes of dark matter interactions, complementing direct-detection searches. We propose using accretion flows of the supermassive black hole as a bolometer for light DM. The kinetic energy of sub-MeV dark matter in the black hole gravitational potential can remain below the thermal energy of the plasma electrons. The colder dark matter population can therefore absorb energy through elastic scattering, cooling the electrons and modifying their emission spectrum. We integrate dark matter cooling into the advection-dominated accretion flow around M87$^{*}$ and solve the full set of thermodynamic equations to obtain the resulting temperature profile and radio-to-millimeter emission. By comparing the predicted spectrum with observations accompanying the Event Horizon Telescope campaign, we use, for the first time, the thermal energy balance of the hot accretion flow to constrain DM-electron scattering, obtaining stringent limits on keV-to-MeV DM for both heavy and light mediators.

papers.title: Probing Dynamical Dark Energy with Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 Cosmic Shear
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34650v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: the unexplained component driving the universe's accelerating expansion; its "equation of state" w describes its pressure-to-density ratio, with w = -1 matching a cosmological constant.
- wCDM vs w0waCDM: a constant w versus a version where w changes over cosmic time (w0 today, wa the rate of change).
- Weak gravitational lensing / cosmic shear: measuring tiny distortions in galaxy shapes caused by intervening matter.
- Tomography: splitting galaxies into redshift (distance) bins to track changes over cosmic time.
- BAO (baryon acoustic oscillations): a standard ruler from sound waves in the early universe, used to measure distances.
- Type Ia supernovae: exploding stars with known brightness, used as cosmic distance markers.
- BBN (Big Bang Nucleosynthesis): theory of light-element formation in the early universe, used here as a prior on baryon density.
- S8: a summary number for how clumpy matter is today.
- Sigma: a standard measure of statistical confidence.
summary.one_liner: A real-space cosmic shear analysis of Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 data, combined with DESI BAO, recalibrated DES supernovae and BBN priors, constrains constant and time-varying dark energy equations of state and the structure growth parameter S8.
summary.plain: Astronomers want to know whether dark energy, the unknown force speeding up the universe's expansion, changes over time. This paper uses the shapes of about 25 million faint galaxies, whose light is slightly bent by matter along the way, together with distance measurements from other sky surveys. The combined result is consistent with a constant dark energy, with a modest 2.4-sigma (roughly 2.4 standard deviations, a weak-to-moderate statistical hint) preference for changing dark energy.
summary.why: If dark energy evolves, that would change our understanding of fundamental physics, so the result matters for judging the signal. The paper also reports that the weak-lensing measure of how clumpy matter is stays stable across the extended models, while the time-varying signal seems to come mainly from the distance measurements. The text does not establish how robust that hint is beyond this one dataset.

papers.abstract: Recent measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and Type Ia Supernovae (SNe) have revealed a preference for a time-evolving dark energy equation of state. Because such dynamical behavior alters both the cosmic expansion history and the late-time growth of structure, weak gravitational lensing measurements can be used to test these extended models. We present an extended analysis of the real-space cosmic shear two-point correlation functions (2PCFs) from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 (HSC-Y3) survey. Using over 25 million galaxies across 416 deg$^2$, divided into four tomographic redshift bins ($0.3 < z \le 1.5$), we constrain both a constant ($w$CDM) and a time-varying ($w_0w_a$CDM) dark energy equation of state. To break the geometric degeneracies inherent in cosmic shear, we combine the HSC-Y3 data with a CMB-independent suite of background distance probes: DESI DR2 BAO, the recalibrated DES five-year SN sample (DOVEKIE), and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) priors. In the $w$CDM paradigm, our joint analysis yields $w =-0.936^{+0.074}_{-0.067}$, consistent with a cosmological constant. Within the $w_0w_a$CDM framework, we find $w_0 =-0.832^{+0.071}_{-0.059}$ and $w_a = -1.23^{+0.66}_{-0.44}$, representing a $2.4\sigma$ preference for dynamical dark energy. Although the unconstrained dark energy parameters reduce the cosmic shear-only $S_8$ constraints to smaller values, our joint multi-probe analysis agrees with the baseline HSC-Y3 $\Lambda$CDM structure growth amplitude. We obtain $S_8 = 0.774^{+0.027}_{-0.034}$ for $w$CDM and $S_8 = 0.772^{+0.031}_{-0.030}$ for $w_0w_a$CDM. Our results demonstrate that the weak lensing amplitude is robust to extended dark energy parameterizations, and that the dynamical dark energy signal is currently driven primarily by the geometric distance ladders, a critical consistency test for next-generation Stage-IV cosmological surveys.

papers.title: Learning to find cosmic filaments with graph neural networks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31494v1

summary.background:
- Cosmic web: the large-scale pattern of galaxies, filaments, walls and voids in the Universe.
- Galaxy survey: a catalog of galaxy positions, which is incomplete and sparse.
- Filament finding: algorithms that trace these threads through galaxy positions.
- Generative model: a model that learns a distribution and can produce new samples from it, here giving many possible filament networks.
- Flow matching: a training method that learns to transform random noise into samples resembling the target data.
- Graph neural network: a neural network operating on nodes and connections, suited to networks of points.
- Conditional model: one whose outputs depend on given inputs, here the observed tracers.
summary.one_liner: A generative model built from flow matching and graph neural networks learns to produce probabilistic samples of cosmic filament networks from sparse galaxy tracer positions.
summary.plain: Astronomers want to map the large-scale threads of matter, called cosmic filaments, that link galaxy clusters together. Galaxy catalogs give only scattered points, so the exact shape of these threads cannot be read off directly. This paper trains a machine-learning model to generate many plausible filament layouts consistent with the galaxies, and reports that the outputs match key statistics of the target filaments while varying across samples.
summary.why: Filaments are a major part of the cosmic web, and a method that reports uncertainty about them could matter for future galaxy surveys. The text describes this as a first step, so its practical value for real survey data is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Inferring the large-scale structure of the Universe from galaxy surveys is a fundamental challenge in cosmology. In particular, cosmic filaments form an extended and geometrically complex network whose underlying structure cannot be reconstructed from discrete galaxy catalogs without uncertainty. We investigate a generative approach to filament finding based on flow matching and graph neural networks. The learned model reproduces key statistical properties of the target filament distribution while generating a distribution over possible filament configurations, demonstrating its ability to model uncertainty. Our work provides a first step towards probabilistic inference of the cosmic web directly from galaxy surveys. More broadly, these results demonstrate the potential of conditional generative models for reconstructing filament-like structures from sparse observational tracers.

papers.title: Resolving the Hubble Tension at $0.1\sigma$ with Early Dark Energy: Key Role of the Highest-redshift Galaxies from JWST Observations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32552v1

summary.background:
- Hubble constant (H0): the present expansion rate of the universe, in km/s per megaparsec.
- Hubble tension: early-universe measurements (CMB) and local measurements (SH0ES, using nearby Cepheid stars and supernovae) give different H0 values.
- Early dark energy (EDE): a hypothetical extra component active briefly before recombination, which changes the expansion history; the axion version is one specific model.
- CMB: the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the early universe.
- DESI baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO): a standard-ruler measurement of galaxy clustering from the DESI survey.
- JWST UV luminosity function: counts of galaxies by ultraviolet brightness at high redshift (very distant, early galaxies); converting these counts to physical quantities requires assuming a reference cosmology.
- Spectral index n_s and running α_s: describe how the primordial density fluctuations vary with physical scale; α_s measures the scale dependence of that tilt.
- σ (sigma): the standard unit of statistical significance; 0.1σ means the two values agree very closely.
summary.one_liner: A cosmology paper arguing that early dark energy (axion EDE) combined with CMB, DESI BAO, and JWST high-redshift galaxy UV luminosity functions can bring the inferred Hubble constant to within 0.1σ of SH0ES, with a running of the spectral index (α_s) pushing H0 higher still.
summary.plain: The universe is expanding at a rate that different measurement methods disagree on: measurements from the early universe give a lower value than direct measurements from nearby stars and galaxies (SH0ES). This paper tests whether a modified model with an extra, short-lived "early dark energy" component, combined with new JWST counts of very distant galaxies, can close that gap. The authors report that it can, with the result depending strongly on how the most distant galaxies are counted and on how the model's power spectrum is allowed to vary with scale.
summary.why: The Hubble tension is one of the most discussed open problems in cosmology, and the paper ties it to new JWST observations of early galaxies and to the settings of the primordial matter spectrum. It is worth watching because the result depends on modelling choices, so it is an interesting proposal rather than a settled resolution; whether it holds up will depend on independent data and reanalyses.

papers.abstract: We show that the Hubble tension can be resolved at the $0.1\sigma$ level within the early dark energy (EDE) framework, with the highest-redshift galaxies from the JWST observations playing a key role. By accounting for the reference cosmologies of the JWST ultraviolet luminosity function measurements and combining them with cosmic microwave background (CMB) and DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data, we obtain $H_0=72.76\pm1.00~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ in the axion EDE model, in excellent agreement with SH0ES at the $0.1\sigma$ level. We find that the enhanced galaxy abundances at $z=11$ and $12.5$ play a key role in driving this result. These observations favor stronger small-scale matter power, which can be accommodated by increasing the primordial scalar spectral index $n_{\rm s}$. Under the CMB constraints, the positive correlations among $n_{\rm s}$, $f_{\rm EDE}$, and $H_0$ lead to a higher inferred $H_0$. Allowing additional scale dependence in the primordial power spectrum through $\alpha_{\rm s}$ yields a positive running at more than $4\sigma$, further increasing $H_0$ to $73.75\pm1.04~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, with its value even exceeding the SH0ES measurement. These results reveal how high-redshift small-scale structure observations influence the inferred $H_0$ through the interplay between the primordial power spectrum and EDE parameter degeneracies.

papers.title: $w_0$ Is All You Need: Field-Level Matching of General Dark Energy Models to $w_0$CDM Simulations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29776v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: an unknown component thought to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe; its equation of state w describes how its pressure relates to its energy density.
- w0CDM: a standard model where w is a single constant value today (w0).
- w(z): a dark energy equation of state that changes with redshift (z, a measure of look-back time).
- CPL parametrization: a common two-parameter form w0 + wa(1-a) for time-varying dark energy.
- N-body simulation: a computer simulation that tracks many particles under gravity to model how cosmic structure forms.
- Power spectrum and bispectrum: statistics measuring how strongly matter clusters at different scales (two-point and three-point correlations).
- Wavelet scattering transform: a summary statistic for non-Gaussian patterns in a field.
- Spectral equivalence: the idea that two models give nearly identical matter fields under a specific matching rule.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes that clustering of matter in general dynamical dark energy models w(z) can be reproduced by a constant-w0 CDM simulation via spectral equivalence, matching comoving distance to the last scattering surface, and tests this with N-body runs including spline-based w(z).
summary.plain: Cosmologists simulate how matter clumps together in the universe, and the outcome depends on the unknown "dark energy" that drives cosmic expansion. This paper asks whether a simpler, constant-strength dark energy simulation can stand in for many more complicated versions. The authors report that, in their simulations, matter patterns from the more complicated models match the simple reference case closely, within a fraction of a percent for the measured statistics.
summary.why: If the matching holds, researchers could test many dark energy models against survey data without running a new set of expensive simulations for each one, which matters for upcoming large sky surveys. The text does not show how well this generalizes beyond the models and statistics tested, so the broader claim remains to be checked by others.

papers.abstract: We show that clustering in general dynamical dark energy models $w(z)$ can be predicted with constant dark energy $w_0\text{CDM}$ models at the field level via spectral equivalence. The prescription of this method requires equating comoving distances to the last scattering surface between predictor and target models, which is equivalent to requiring equal recent background expansion history averages. Dark energy models with the same distance thus form approximate equivalence classes, with nearly identical matter fields. To test the precision of spectral equivalence beyond the CPL parametrization, we run $N$-body simulations with various dynamical dark energy models, including spline-based $w(z)$, all matched to a single $w_0\text{CDM}$ run. Our measurements show that the power spectra of all matched dark energies agree with the predictor within $0.2\%$ up to $k = 0.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ and within $0.6\%$ up to $k = 1\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We also compare the non-Gaussian information contained in the simulated fields. Bispectra differ by at most $0.26\%$ across all runs up to $k = 0.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ and $1.75\%$ up to $k = 1\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, while wavelet scattering transform coefficients are all within $0.05\%$. The decorrelation, $1 - r^2$, between each matched field and the predictor stays below $0.006\%$ up to $k = 1\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We run a toy power spectrum analysis in the CPL parametrization demonstrating that a $w_0$-only emulator could produce the same posterior without any knowledge of the full $w_0w_a$ model. This matching prescription thus offers a new tool to constrain dynamical dark energy models with arbitrary equations of state at the field level, without running additional simulation suites.

papers.title: Analytic $k$-essence Inflation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30846v1

summary.background:
- Inflation: a brief period of very rapid, accelerating expansion of the early universe, thought to seed the large-scale structure we observe.
- Scalar field: a hypothetical field whose value varies in space and time; inflation is often modeled with one.
- k-essence: a generalization in which the field's energy depends on a kinetic term X (roughly, how fast the field changes) in a non-standard, nonlinear way.
- Slow-roll assumption: the common approximation that the field changes slowly, used to simplify inflation equations.
- Hubble rate: the expansion rate of the universe; e-folding: a factor of e (about 2.7) growth in the scale factor.
- Sound speed of perturbations: the speed at which small density ripples propagate; if it is wrong, instabilities can arise.
- Pressure singularity: a point where pressure blows up in the model's equations, a sign the model breaks down there.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives a fully analytic k-essence inflation model with kinetic term K(X)=X^n/X_s^(n-1) and a tracking condition, where constant sound speed avoids gradient instabilities and a pressure singularity after inflation is argued to be classically avoided once radiation and cold dark matter are included.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model of the very early universe in which a rapid expansion (inflation) is driven by a field whose energy depends on its motion in an unusual way, called k-essence. Earlier versions of such models needed approximations built into the equations; here the authors find solutions that can be written in closed form as functions of cosmic time. They report that the model fits the observational limits on inflation, but that its expansion develops a mathematical pressure singularity a few e-foldings after inflation ends. Using numerical arguments, they claim this singularity is avoided once ordinary matter (radiation and cold dark matter) is included.
summary.why: Analytic solutions are useful because they let researchers check predictions and stability without relying on numerical simulation or the slow-roll shortcut. The reported singularity and its possible resolution by ordinary matter are the points that a reader would need to weigh, since the claim rests on numerical arguments given in the text. Its connection to observations is limited to the statement that the inflation indices depend only on n and m.

papers.abstract: In this work we develop a fully analytic $k$-essence inflation solution which is compatible with the observational constraints on inflation, without the need for the slow-roll assumption being imposed dynamically in the field equations. The analytic solution is obtained for a kinetic scalar sector of the form $K(X)= \frac{X^n}{X_s^{n-1}}$ and for the scalar field satisfying a tracking condition $\dot{\phi}^2=\gamma H^{-m}$. For this class of theories, the sound speed of the primordial curvature perturbations is constant, so no gradient instabilities occur in the theory. The Hubble rate, the scale factor and the scalar field can be analytically expressed as functions of the cosmic time, and the observational indices of inflation depend solely on the parameters $n$ and $m$. The resulting evolution is inflationary and it develops a pressure singularity a few $e$-foldings after the end of inflation. However, using qualitative and quantitative numerical arguments, we show that the pressure singularity is classically avoided when the matter fluids of radiation and cold dark matter are taken into account.

papers.title: Beyond the Peak: Constraining early dark energy with the damping tail
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27069v1

summary.background:
- The Hubble tension: measurements of the universe's current expansion rate (H0) from the early universe (CMB) and from nearby stars and supernovae disagree.
- Early dark energy (EDE): a hypothetical scalar field that briefly contributes energy shortly before recombination, changing the sound-wave scale in the early universe; proposed as one way to ease the tension.
- Scalar field and potential: a field whose energy depends on its value, like a ball rolling in a landscape; the "potential" is that landscape's shape.
- Axion-like and alpha-attractor potentials: two classes of field-landscape shapes used in model building.
- Observational datasets: CMB (light from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang), baryon acoustic oscillations (large-scale galaxy patterns), and supernovae (distance markers).
- High-ℓ CMB: the small-angle, fine-scale part of the microwave sky map.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that the post-peak "tail" of an early dark energy scalar field, not just its peak amplitude and location, carries observable information about a multiscale potential (axion-like plus alpha-attractor regimes) and can improve fits to high-ℓ CMB data and the inferred H0.
summary.plain: Cosmologists have proposed an "early dark energy" component that briefly existed before the universe's recombination era, which might ease a disagreement between two ways of measuring how fast the universe expands. This paper focuses on the part of that energy's behavior after its main burst, which the authors call the "tail," and builds a simple model in which different parts of a field's energy landscape control its motion. Fitting the model to cosmic microwave background, galaxy-clustering (baryon acoustic oscillation), and supernova data, they report a better match to the high-resolution microwave data and a higher best-fit expansion rate.
summary.why: The Hubble tension is a well-known discrepancy in cosmology, and the paper suggests that a previously overlooked feature of early dark energy models could help distinguish between them and partly address it. The text does not establish how decisive the improvement is, and the claims would need independent checks against other datasets.

papers.abstract: Early dark energy is commonly characterized by the amplitude and location of its primary energy-injection peak. We show that its post-peak evolution, which we call the \emph{EDE tail}, provides an additional observable probe of the underlying scalar dynamics and can materially affect its ability to alleviate the Hubble tension. We construct a simple phenomenological framework in which distinct regions of a multiscale scalar potential govern the dynamics at different field scales. As a representative realization, we consider a potential that combines axion-like and $\alpha$-attractor-like regimes, thereby allowing the EDE tail to be reshaped through reflection and asymmetric oscillations. Confronting this framework with cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillation, and supernova observations, we find an improved fit to the high-$\ell$ CMB data together with a higher inferred bestfit $H_0$. Our results show that the EDE tail retains observable information about the underlying scalar potential that is not captured by the conventional peak parameters alone. This provides a complementary route for constructing and observationally distinguishing EDE scenarios, and potentially for further alleviating the Hubble tension.

papers.title: Dark Energy Based on Modified Gravity: Where the Future Lies?
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27228v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: the unknown component driving the universe's accelerated expansion.
- Phantom vs. quintessence: phantom dark energy has an equation-of-state value below -1, quintessence stays above it; the text says the behavior may have shifted between them.
- DESI: a large galaxy survey whose data constrain dark energy.
- F(R) gravity: a modification of Einstein's general relativity in which the gravitational Lagrangian depends on the Ricci scalar curvature R.
- Scalar field: an extra field whose value can vary across space and time; here it carries the potential barrier.
- Ghost graviton: a mode with negative kinetic energy, which signals instability.
- Peculiar velocities and the kSZ (kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich) effect: observable signatures used to test gravity and dark energy on large scales.
- Fine-tuning: choosing special starting values for parameters to get a desired outcome.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that realistic F(R) gravity models fitted to DESI-era dark energy data can drift into anti-gravity or ghost-graviton regimes in the future, and proposes a scalar-field potential barrier at small curvature to prevent this without fine-tuning initial conditions.
summary.plain: Recent measurements hint that dark energy, the mysterious cause of the universe's accelerating expansion, may have behaved in an unusual "phantom" way in the recent past and then switched to a more ordinary form. Some modified-gravity theories fit these data, but this paper finds that some of them may eventually lead to unphysical behavior, such as repulsive "anti-gravity." The authors propose adding a barrier to a scalar field that keeps the universe out of that future, and suggest ways to test this with galaxy motion and the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect.
summary.why: It bears on whether the dark-energy models that currently fit DESI survey data are physically sound over the long term, a question that matters for the future of cosmology. The text does not show how strongly the proposed barrier would be supported by data, so its practical weight is still open.

papers.abstract: Based on current observational data, there is a strong possibility that dark energy was in a phantom regime in the near past, and a transition from a phantom to a quintessential regime may have occurred. Since then, many scenarios compatible with the DESI data have been proposed. In particular, there exist several realistic models in the framework of $F(R)$ gravity. In this paper, we show that such realistic models of $F(R)$ gravity may produce an anti-gravity or ghost graviton in the future. The problem could be avoided by further changing the parameters and fine-tuning the initial conditions, but we propose to introduce a potential barrier of the scalar field for the small scalar curvature region, which prevents the Universe from evolving into the anti-gravity or having a ghost graviton region, without the fine-tuning of the initial conditions. We also discuss how this regime can be tested using peculiar velocity and kSZ effect probes.

papers.title: Breaking the background and linear degeneracies: Using nonlinear clustering to discriminate between dark energy models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26460v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: the unknown component thought to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe.
- Equation of state w(a): the ratio of a dark energy's pressure to its density, which may change over cosmic time (a is the scale factor, a stand-in for time).
- Sound speed squared: sets how quickly disturbances spread through a fluid; here it is a time-dependent quantity.
- Linear vs. nonlinear perturbations: small density ripples grow in a simple way at first; once they become dense, the behaviour must be simulated in full.
- Spherical collapse: a simplified model of a clump of matter contracting under its own gravity to form a halo.
- Dark matter halo: a dense clump of dark matter in which galaxies and clusters form.
summary.one_liner: Shows that dark energy models with identical equation-of-state w(a) and effective sound speed can still differ in nonlinear spherical-collapse simulations of clustering dark energy, with the local sound speed identified as the main driver.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether the standard way of describing dark energy, a single number for how its pressure relates to its density plus a sound-speed value, fully pins down how dark energy behaves. Using a new fully nonlinear fluid framework, the authors simulate the collapse of large clumps of matter in two dark energy models that share those same two descriptors. They report that the dark energy density at the centre of cluster-sized halos can differ by up to 50% between the two models.
summary.why: If the result holds, small-scale structure such as galaxy clusters could carry information that large-scale measurements miss, which would be a new route to telling dark energy models apart. The text does not show observational tests, so the practical impact is still an open question.

papers.abstract: We show that the traditional approach of parameterizing the background and linear-perturbation evolutions, through the equation-of-state parameter $w(a)$ and a time-dependent sound speed squared $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, does not fully specify the cosmological behavior of dark energy theories. Using a new, fully nonlinear fluid framework, we perform spherical-collapse simulations of two clustering dark energy models with identical $w(a)$ and $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, finding that their central dark-energy densities differ by up to 50\% for cluster-sized dark matter halos. We identify the departure of the local sound speed from $\bar{c}_s$ as the main driver of these differences. In contrast, all other theory-specific quantities in the fluid equations can be described by their background values to a very good approximation. The results demonstrate that nonlinear structure formation encodes critical additional information about the underlying dark energy theory, opening an avenue for discriminating between models using observables on small scales.

papers.title: Splitting the action: A fully nonlinear fluid method for clustering dark energy
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26461v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: a hypothesized component causing the universe's accelerated expansion; its "perturbations" are small local density variations.
- k-essence: a class of dark-energy theories where the energy depends on the kinetic term of a scalar field; the "sound speed" sets how quickly pressure perturbations propagate.
- Clustering: whether dark energy gathers into lumps like dark matter, rather than staying smooth.
- Nonlinear regime: when density contrasts are large, so linear approximations break down (e.g., inside collapsing halos).
- Spherical collapse: a simplified model of a uniform spherical overdensity collapsing under gravity, used as a test case.
- Action: a quantity from which field equations are derived; splitting it means separating the kinetic and potential contributions.
- Fluid method / SPH: ways of simulating matter as a fluid, either on grids or with particles.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a fully nonlinear fluid method, built by splitting the dark-energy action into kinetic and potential parts, and uses spherical-collapse simulations of two k-essence models to study dark-energy clustering around dark-matter halos.
summary.plain: Dark energy is the unknown component thought to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe, and some versions of it may clump together under gravity like matter does. Existing computer methods for modeling this clumping rely on approximations whose accuracy in the strongly nonlinear regime is unclear. The authors propose a new way to write the equations of dark energy as a fluid, and test it on simplified spherical collapses of two example models.
summary.why: Simulating how dark energy clusters on small scales matters for interpreting future cosmological surveys, but the text only shows a proof-of-concept on spherical collapse, not full 3D cosmological results. The authors frame it as groundwork for later particle-based (SPH) simulations, which the text does not demonstrate.

papers.abstract: While the background evolution of dark energy is relatively straightforward to model, its perturbations, especially on nonlinear scales, generally require significantly more sophisticated treatment. Existing simulation methods for clustering dark energy --- a large class of interesting theories which are until now not well studied --- usually rely on grid-based solvers and perturbatively derived equations, whose validity in the nonlinear regime remains unknown. In this paper, we introduce a novel fluid method based on splitting the dark energy action into two parts: a kinetic part and a potential part. The resulting fluid equations are fully nonlinear and not reliant on simplifying approximations, making them suitable to describe the small-scale evolution of clustering dark energy theories, such as $k$-essence models with small sound speeds. We demonstrate the numerical implementation of this framework through spherical-collapse simulations of two representative $k$-essence models, evolving dark matter and dark energy simultaneously. The simulations are able to follow the development of dark-energy density perturbations throughout halo collapse, to $\mathcal{O}(\textrm{1}-10)$. By investigating their dependence on the dark-energy sound speed and dark-matter halo mass, we illustrate how dark-energy clustering responds to variations in the competing effects of pressure support and gravitational pull. These results demonstrate the applicability of this new framework to study nonlinear dark-energy clustering across a range of physical conditions, providing the foundation for its future extension to fully three-dimensional cosmological simulations through particle-based algorithms such as smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH).

papers.title: New Observational Insights into Generalised Axion-Like Dark Energy
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24900v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: the unknown cause of the universe's accelerating expansion; the simplest version is a constant (ΛCDM model).
- Quintessence: a dark energy version where a scalar field (a field with a single value at each point in space and time) changes over time.
- Axion-like potential: the shape of the field's energy landscape, borrowed from particle physics ideas about axions.
- Tracking regime: a phase where the field's behaviour follows the background energy, so its starting value matters less.
- Coincidence problem: the puzzle of why dark energy and matter have comparable densities now.
- Datasets: CMB distance priors (imprint of the early universe), BAO (regular clustering of galaxies), Type Ia supernovae and gamma-ray bursts (standard-brightness distance markers), cosmic chronometers (ages of old galaxies), SH0ES (local measurement of the expansion rate, the "Hubble tension").
- Parameter inference: fitting model settings to data and comparing fit quality with ΛCDM.
summary.one_liner: A quintessence (dynamical dark energy) model with a generalised axion-like potential and a tracking regime is confronted with background-expansion data (CMB distance priors, BAO, Type Ia supernovae, SH0ES, cosmic chronometers, gamma-ray bursts) and compared statistically with ΛCDM.
summary.plain: This paper studies a model in which the mysterious force speeding up the universe's expansion comes from a field that slowly changes over time, rather than from a fixed constant. The authors test this model against several sets of astronomical measurements, such as supernova brightness records and sound-wave patterns left from the early universe. They check how well it fits the data, whether it helps reconcile conflicting measurements, and how it compares with the standard model.
summary.why: The model is presented as addressing the "coincidence problem" (why dark energy and matter densities are of similar size today) without needing carefully tuned starting conditions. Whether it is worth attention depends on the statistical results, which the summary text does not report, so the value of the work is not yet clear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: We consider a quintessence model based on a generalised axion-like scalar field potential, originally introduced as a phenomenological framework to describe the late-time accelerated expansion of the Universe. The model exhibits a tracking regime that alleviates the coincidence problem and naturally leads to a phase of late-time acceleration driven by an effective cosmological constant, without requiring fine-tuning of the scalar field initial conditions. In this work, we confront the background cosmological evolution of this model with current observations by performing a parameter inference analysis using cosmic microwave background distance priors, baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, Type Ia supernovae, the SH0ES distance ladder, cosmic chronometers, and gamma-ray bursts. This analysis allows us to assess the observational viability of the model, its ability to reconcile different cosmological datasets, and its statistical performance relative to $Λ$CDM.

papers.title: Deconstructing the cosmic baryon distribution with fast radio bursts
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24838v1

summary.background:
- Baryons: ordinary matter (protons, neutrons, electrons), as opposed to dark matter.
- Large-scale structure: the web of voids, filaments and galaxy clusters (haloes) formed by gravity over cosmic time.
- Fast radio bursts (FRBs): brief, bright radio flashes from distant sources; plasma along the path delays low frequencies more than high ones. The size of that delay, the dispersion measure, tells you how many electrons lie along the path.
- Density estimator: here, the ratio of electron number to total matter density.
- IllustrisTNG: a large cosmological hydrodynamical simulation used as a test universe with known answers.
- Euclid: a European space telescope survey; a "Euclid-like mock catalogue" is a simulated galaxy survey with similar properties.
- Bayesian framework: a method that combines a model with data and reports a range of plausible values with uncertainties.
- Omega_b f_ion: the cosmic baryon density times the fraction of baryons that are ionised, a standard cosmological quantity.
summary.one_liner: Using IllustrisTNG simulations, the authors combine fast radio burst dispersion measures with a Euclid-like galaxy mock catalogue in a Bayesian framework to estimate the electron-to-matter density ratio across eight large-scale-structure density bins and recover the ionised baryon density.
summary.plain: Most of the ordinary matter in the universe (baryons) is spread out so thinly that it is hard to see directly. This paper uses flashes of radio waves from distant space, called fast radio bursts, which get slightly delayed by the electrons they pass through, to map where that matter sits. The authors test the method on a computer simulation and on a mock galaxy survey, and report that it recovers the total ionised matter density to within a few percent and tracks gas fractions in voids, filaments and haloes.
summary.why: Knowing where baryons are matters for interpreting gravitational lensing, galaxy evolution and the cosmic microwave background in current and future surveys. The work is at the simulation and mock-data stage, so its value for real observations depends on how well these idealised tests carry over to actual sky data; the text does not address that directly.

papers.abstract: The precise distribution of baryons in the Universe remains an open question in cosmology, as their highly diffuse nature hinders direct observation. However, mapping it is integral for precision cosmology in studies of gravitational lensing, galaxy evolution and the cosmic microwave background with current and upcoming surveys. We use fast radio bursts (FRBs) and their dispersion measures (DMs) to probe and localise this baryon distribution in the large-scale structure (LSS). Using IllustrisTNG simulations, we classify the LSS into eight bins of increasing matter density, analogous to voids, filaments, and haloes. We model the DM contribution from each substructure and compare it with the simulated DMs to infer the density estimator, the ratio of electron number to total matter density. The resulting overdetermined system is solved in a Bayesian framework with a simulation-physics-informed model. To demonstrate observational applicability, we create a Euclid-like mock galaxy catalogue and build a density estimator based on luminous matter along FRB sightlines. We apply a bias correction for the underlying dark matter distribution and compare the two density estimators to recover the electron number density across the eight bins. Electrons are predominantly localised in low-density regions, while the ensemble mean across all bins aligns with the global theoretical estimate. Combining the FRB and galaxy density estimators, we recover the density of ionised baryons as $Ω_b f_{ion} = 0.0455^{+0.0028}_{-0.0026}$ (simulation: 0.0462), corresponding to $Ω_b = 0.0479^{+0.0029}_{-0.0027}$ for $f_{ion}=0.95$. Our bin-wise electron density estimate reproduces the simulation ground truth to within 10 per cent and gives gas fractions of $0.186 \pm 0.012$, $0.179 \pm 0.015$ and $0.046 \pm 0.014$ in voids, filaments and haloes, against ground truths of 0.167, 0.173 and 0.067.

papers.title: Using the 0i Einstein equation to break dark-sector degeneracies
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22498v1

summary.background:
- ΛCDM: the standard "concordance" model of cosmology, with dark energy (a constant-like term), cold dark matter, and general relativity.
- Cosmological tension: measurements from different methods or epochs that disagree with ΛCDM predictions.
- Modified gravity: changing Einstein's general relativity on cosmic scales.
- Dark energy and dark matter: the unseen components that drive cosmic expansion and clump around galaxies.
- Degeneracy: when different underlying causes produce the same observed effect, so they cannot be told apart.
- Gravitational slip: a comparison of two gravitational potentials; a nonzero value signals departure from general relativity.
- Euler equation: an equation describing how matter flows under gravity, used to track how matter moves.
- Einstein equations: the field equations of general relativity linking spacetime curvature to energy and matter; the "0i" component is one of their parts (mixing time and space directions) that is usually not used in tests.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that current cosmological tests cannot separate modified gravity, dark energy, and dark matter explanations of deviations from ΛCDM, and proposes three tests built only on observables, including the 0i Einstein equation, to break these degeneracies.
summary.plain: Astronomers have found some measurements that do not quite fit the standard model of the universe. This paper asks whether the mismatch comes from gravity itself, from dark energy, or from dark matter, and argues that today's tests cannot tell these apart because they rely on quantities that cannot be directly observed. The authors propose three tests that use only directly observable quantities, and they say that combining them, including a rarely tested equation (the 0i Einstein equation), can distinguish the three possibilities.
summary.why: If the cosmic tensions are real, knowing which part of physics needs changing matters a great deal, so a way to separate these explanations is useful. The text describes the proposal and its motivation but does not show results from applying the tests to data, so its practical payoff is not yet demonstrated.

papers.abstract: Over the past decade, cosmological observations have started to challenge the $Λ$CDM model. If these tensions persist, they immediately raise one fundamental question: what new physics could be responsible for them? More specifically, do these deviations arise from a modification of gravity, from an evolving or clustering dark energy component, or from dark matter properties beyond the cold dark matter paradigm? In this paper we show that, with current methods, any observed deviation can always be attributed to more than one sector, preventing us from determining if the tension is due to gravity, dark energy or dark matter. The main reason is that current tests rely on unobservable quantities. These quantities are then either related to observables by assuming the validity of specific equations, or compared with theoretical predictions computed within a given class of theories. Both approaches inevitably break the model independence of the tests, leading to degeneracies between gravity, dark energy, and dark matter. To overcome this limitation, we construct a set of three tests that rely only on observable quantities and that, when combined, can distinguish between the three sectors. We show that the $0i$ Einstein equation -- which is never tested in standard analyses -- adds crucial information to that provided by the gravitational slip equation and the Euler equation.

papers.title: Probing Velocity-Dependent WIMP Dark Matter Annihilation in Large-Scale Structure
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22387v1

summary.background:
- WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles): a leading hypothetical dark matter candidate that could annihilate into gamma rays.
- Annihilation cross section: a measure of how likely two dark matter particles are to destroy each other; here it is written as a power law in relative velocity, with the exponent n setting the dependence.
- s-wave (n=0): rate independent of speed; p-wave and d-wave: rate rising with speed; Sommerfeld-like (n=-1): rate enhanced at low speed.
- Unresolved gamma-ray background (UGRB): the diffuse gamma-ray glow from sources too faint to be individually resolved, such as measured by Fermi LAT.
- Cross-correlation: a statistic measuring how similar two sky maps are at matching positions, here gamma rays versus galaxies.
- Halo model: a framework that describes dark matter as clumps (halos) and computes clustering from how those halos are distributed.
- Large-scale structure: the cosmic web of galaxies and dark matter on very large scales.
summary.one_liner: A generalized halo-model forecast of how velocity-dependent WIMP dark matter annihilation (power-law in relative velocity, n = -1, 0, 2, 4) would imprint on the cross-correlation between the unresolved gamma-ray background and the 2MRS galaxy catalog.
summary.plain: Dark matter may be made of particles that sometimes destroy each other, releasing gamma rays, and how fast they collide may change how much they do so. This paper studies how such collisions, if they depend on speed, would show up in the faint gamma-ray glow from the whole sky when it is compared with the map of where galaxies sit. The authors model four cases and forecast how well a combined gamma-ray and galaxy survey comparison could constrain the annihilation rate.
summary.why: Most earlier searches assumed the annihilation rate does not depend on speed, so this work asks whether different particle physics models leave distinguishable fingerprints in large-scale structure. It is a forecast built from the text alone; the text does not report any actual measured detection, so its practical reach depends on how well the assumptions hold.

papers.abstract: The unresolved gamma-ray background (UGRB) provides a promising avenue for probing the cosmological annihilation of weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter through its cross-correlation with large-scale structure (LSS). While most previous studies have assumed a velocity-independent (s-wave) annihilation cross section, many well-motivated particle physics models predict annihilation rates that depend on the relative velocity of dark matter particles. In this work, we develop a generalized halo-model framework to investigate the cosmological signatures of velocity-dependent WIMP annihilation. Parameterizing the velocity-weighted annihilation cross section as $σv_{\rm rel}\propto v_{\rm rel}^{n}$, we consider four representative cases corresponding to Sommerfeld-like (n=-1), s-wave (n=0), p-wave (n=2), and d-wave (n=4) annihilation. We show that velocity dependence modifies not only the overall annihilation emission but also the halo population dominating the signal, leading to distinct effective halo biases, redshift distributions, and angular clustering properties. As a result, different annihilation mechanisms leave characteristic signatures in the UGRB-LSS cross-correlation that cannot be captured by the overall gamma-ray intensity alone. As an illustration of the formalism, we perform a statistical forecast for the cross-correlation between the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) UGRB and the Two Micron All Sky Survey Redshift Survey (2MRS) galaxy catalog and derive the projected sensitivities to the velocity-independent annihilation coefficient for these four annihilation scenarios. Our results demonstrate that cosmological cross-correlations provide a powerful and complementary probe of velocity-dependent dark matter annihilation, offering a new avenue for constraining the particle physics of dark matter through its imprints on large-scale structure.

papers.title: On the origin of Milky Way binary black holes with LISA
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21337v1

summary.background:
- Primordial black holes: black holes formed in the very early universe, not from collapsed stars.
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies, inferred from its gravity.
- Binary black holes: two black holes orbiting each other; their merging or inspiral emits gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime.
- LISA: a planned space-based gravitational-wave observatory (a set of three spacecraft) expected to launch in the 2030s.
- Fisher-matrix forecast: a standard statistical shortcut for estimating how precisely an instrument could measure parameters, without running full data analysis.
- Monte Carlo realizations: many randomly generated mock datasets used to estimate how often an outcome occurs.
- Overlap ratio (ln B): a log-odds style score comparing how well each binary's sky location matches the stellar versus dark-matter density; negative values favour the dark-matter picture here.
summary.one_liner: A Fisher-matrix forecast for a 10-year LISA mission proposes using the 3D sky localization of Galactic binary black holes, compared against stellar versus dark-matter density profiles via an overlap ratio, to tell primordial black holes from stellar-origin ones.
summary.plain: Black holes that formed in the early universe, called primordial black holes, might make up some of the invisible dark matter in our galaxy. Black holes made from dying stars should instead sit mostly where the galaxy's visible stars are. This paper proposes telling the two apart by pinning down where pairs of black holes orbiting each other in the Milky Way are located, using a future space gravitational-wave detector called LISA. The authors simulated 1000 mock 10-year missions and found that a few well-located pairs would usually separate the two scenarios.
summary.why: If it works, this gives a way to test whether primordial black holes contribute to dark matter that does not depend on seeing them directly. The result depends on modelling choices and simulated data rather than real detections, so it is a forecast, not an observed finding.

papers.abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may constitute a fraction of dark matter, but distinguishing them from black holes of stellar origin remains a major challenge. We propose a new method based on the three-dimensional localization of Galactic Binary Black Holes (BBHs) by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). While stellar-origin BBHs are expected to be associated with the stellar distribution of the Milky Way, PBHs may trace its more extended dark matter halo. We introduce a spatial overlap ratio that compares the gravitational-wave localization of each binary with the normalized stellar and dark matter density profiles. Using a Fisher-matrix forecast and 1000 Monte Carlo realizations of a 10-year LISA mission, we find that detecting three BBHs with an overlap ratio ln B < 0 occurs in approximately 99% of simulations where BBHs trace dark matter, but in fewer than 0.1% of simulations where they follow the stellar distribution, even when including a stellar halo containing 3% of the Galactic stellar mass. These results suggest that the localization of only a few Galactic BBHs could provide strong evidence for a primordial population, offering an independent test of their possible contribution to dark matter.

papers.title: Probing baryonic feedback using fast radio bursts and galaxy surveys
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18512v1

summary.background:
- Fast radio bursts (FRBs): millisecond radio flashes from far away; their dispersion measure (DM) is the total amount of free electrons along the line of sight.
- Baryons: ordinary matter (gas, stars); feedback is energy from stars and black holes that blows gas out of galaxies, changing its distribution.
- Weak lensing: measuring tiny distortions of background galaxy shapes caused by intervening mass; Stage IV surveys are the next generation of such projects.
- Power spectrum / cross-spectrum: statistics that show how strongly fluctuations cluster at different physical scales, and how two maps correlate.
- Hybrid Effective Field Theory (HEFT): a computational approach for modeling how galaxies and matter cluster, extended here to electrons.
- Padé model: a parameterized functional form used to describe the feedback effect.
- Kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect: a distortion of the cosmic microwave background caused by hot gas moving along the line of sight, another gas probe the paper compares against.
- Bias and stochasticity: how well a tracer (galaxies, electrons) follows the underlying matter, including random scatter.
summary.one_liner: Forecasts how well cross-correlating future fast radio burst dispersion-measure catalogs with galaxy surveys, modeled with Hybrid Effective Field Theory and a Padé feedback model, could constrain baryonic feedback relevant to Stage IV weak lensing.
summary.plain: Fast radio bursts are brief flashes of radio waves from distant sources, and the way their signals are delayed as they pass through gas reveals how much ionized matter lies along the path. The paper asks whether many such bursts, combined with galaxy maps, can show how gas is pushed around by galaxy formation (called baryonic feedback). The authors report that this cross-correlation looks more promising than other options they compare, and that the main limits would come from how electrons and galaxies relate to each other, not from how galaxies trace matter.
summary.why: Baryonic feedback is a major uncertainty for weak lensing surveys that map dark matter through galaxy shape distortions, so an independent probe could help calibrate it. The text is a forecast rather than a measurement, so the actual usefulness depends on future FRB surveys delivering the expected data.

papers.abstract: The dispersion measure (DM) of fast radio bursts (FRB) provides a noisy measure of the free-electron column density to the burst. With next-generation FRB surveys the number of bursts will drastically increase and measurements of the baryon distribution will be possible on the Mpc scales most relevant to Stage IV weak lensing surveys. Comparing the DM auto-spectrum, DM-shear cross-spectrum and the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, we argue that the cross-correlation of FRB catalogs with galaxy surveys offers many advantages. Hybrid Effective Field Theory (HEFT), often used in large-scale structure cosmology, is capable of modeling the clustering of electrons jointly with galaxies and matter to small scales. Using HEFT with the Padé model of baryonic feedback, we forecast that next-generation FRB surveys (combined with galaxy samples) will be able to constrain feedback at a level informative for Stage IV weak lensing surveys. In particular we should not be limited by modeling the manner in which galaxies trace the matter field. Rather constraints of the higher-order electron biases and the electron-galaxy cross-stochasticity provide the dominant limitation, and are an obvious target for improvement in order to reach percent-level constraints. The same measurements also provide a valuable means of constraining feedback in hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation in a way that is not tied to the modeling of particular galaxy samples.
